verdict.root_cause: PlaceOrder fails because cartservice returns errors on GetCart. Failing traces terminate at the checkoutservice -> cartservice GetCart span with ERROR status, propagating up through checkoutservice PlaceOrder, frontend PlaceOrder and the frontend HTTP root, which explains the simultaneous checkoutservice/frontend/loadgenerator alerts [tr_f7268c5a7c45]. The mode is fast rejection, not a stall: failing traces finish in ~2.7-3.3ms and payment, email, currency, shipping and productcatalog children are never reached [tr_f7268c5a7c45]. Checkout logs show the same cut point from the other side - intake lines continue to the end of the window while payment, email and message-write completion lines vanish [tr_ba24729e4180]. Checkoutservice itself is healthy: alive, serving continuously, error ratio below its own baseline, no change on record [tr_f010059645e4][tr_fd469f4c51d8]. No dispatch ever touched cartservice, so the mechanism inside it is unmeasured and I will not name one.
verdict.reasoning: Localization is well supported; mechanism is not. Traces put ERROR status on exactly one edge - checkoutservice -> cartservice GetCart - while every other checkout dependency completes normally in the traces that reach it, ruling out payment, email, currency, productcatalog and shipping as origin [tr_f7268c5a7c45]. Logs independently predict the same break point, after intake and before any post-cart step, with no crash or restart records [tr_ba24729e4180]. Checkout is cleared as origin: its error ratio moved down rather than up with no step at onset, it never stopped serving, and no deploy, config push or flag flip is recorded for it [tr_f010059645e4][tr_fd469f4c51d8]. Fault class stays unknown because fast-failure at the cart hop is equally consistent with cartservice exhausting connections to its cache backend, a wrong cache endpoint or credential, or a bad cartservice artifact - and zero evidence was collected on cartservice to choose among them. Restart is the lowest-risk first action given no change is on record; it is provisional, not a diagnosis.
open_questions: No dispatch of any kind ran against cartservice - its logs, metrics, saturation and change history are unexamined; that gap is what would decide fault_class.
Both change queries started at the incident timestamp and ran forward at hops=0, so pre-onset changes and any change to cartservice were never looked for [tr_fd469f4c51d8][tr_6716b53e4284].

The gRPC status code on the failing GetCart was never captured, and checkout's error ratio was already bursty in the baseline, so it is not firmly established that cart errors began at 17:58:45 [tr_ba24729e4180][tr_f010059645e4].

alternatives.root_cause: cartservice's cache/storage backend is refusing or exhausting connections, and cartservice fails GetCart fast as a result.
alternatives.why_not: Plausible and consistent with fast failure, but no cartservice or cache metrics, logs, or saturation data were collected, so naming exhaustion as the mechanism would be unsupported.

alternatives.root_cause: A pre-onset change to cartservice (wrong cache address, credential, or artifact) broke GetCart.
alternatives.why_not: The change queries were scoped to checkoutservice only and began at onset, so no change record for cartservice was ever retrieved either way [tr_6716b53e4284].

proposal.expected_effect: No action is proposed, so the expected effect is that PlaceOrder error traces continue to terminate at the checkoutservice -> cartservice GetCart span with ERROR status, and checkout logs continue to show intake-only sequences, until cartservice itself is actually examined. The next step is observation, not remediation: a metric_baseline on cartservice error ratio, a logql_query on cartservice, and a change_history query on cartservice with a window that starts several hours BEFORE 17:58:45 (both existing change queries started at the incident timestamp and ran forward at hops=0, so they cannot see a pre-onset change to cartservice). Those three results would show whether the mechanism is process state, saturation, or a change - which is exactly what decides between restart_service, revert_config, and rollback_image.
proposal.if_wrong: This abstention is wrong if cartservice is in a state that is degrading further and cheap to clear - e.g. if a cartservice query returns crash-loop/restart evidence or OOM-kill lines, which would meet restart_service's precondition directly. It is also wrong if the incident is severe enough that the cost of continued PlaceOrder failure exceeds the cost of a blind recreate. Either of those would be visible in evidence this board does not yet contain: no dispatch of any kind ran against cartservice, so its logs, metrics, saturation and change history are all unexamined.
proposal.risk: The abstention's risk is prolonged customer-facing checkout failure while the diagnostic dispatches run. The risk of the alternative - the synthesizer's named restart of cartservice - is higher and is why I decline it: restart_service is irreversible and requires evidence pointing at process state, and there is none for cartservice. If the real trigger is a pre-onset config or image change to cartservice (never queried), a restart recreates the container on the same bad config, destroys the in-process cart cache and any process-state evidence, resets uptime and restart counters, and makes the subsequent change-history investigation harder while fixing nothing. A restart that appears to help for one poll cycle would also falsely raise confidence in an unmeasured diagnosis.
proposal.blast_radius: None from this proposal - no service is touched. For contrast, the restart I am declining would land on cartservice, whose inbound edge in this incident is checkoutservice (and frontend's cart-view path); checkoutservice PlaceOrder and frontend would see connection resets for the duration of the recreate, on top of the errors they already see, and loadgenerator would register them.

triage_judgement.reasoning: Critical alerts hit checkoutservice and frontend simultaneously along with the load generator, which is a user-facing failure I cannot dismiss. No open incidents to attribute it to, and the simultaneous onset across a shared dependency fan-out gives no clear fault class yet.
